title: Section 82 — Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife

content.overview: BNS s. 82 — Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife. BNS restatement of IPC 494. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 494. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 82 is the rule on “Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife”. The section provides that (1) Whoever, having a husband or wife living, marries in any case in which such marriage is void by reason of its taking place during the life of such husband or wife, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 82 exists so that “Marrying again during lifetime of husband or wife” has a closed legal test in Chapter V — Of Offences Against Woman and Child. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Sexual offences, assault, marriage, miscarriage, and offences against the child — placed first among the offence chapters.

The provision in detail
82. (1) Whoever, having a husband or wife living, marries in any case in which such marriage is void by reason of its taking place during the life of such husband or wife, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine

Essential ingredients
1. (1) Whoever, having a husband or wife living, marries in any case in which such marriage is void by reason of its taking place during the life of such husband or wife, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine

Exceptions, limitations and provisos
Exception.—This sub-section does not extend to any person whose marriage with such husband or wife has been declared void by a Court of competent jurisdiction, nor to any person who contracts a marriage during the life of a former husband or wife, if such husband or wife, at the time of the subsequent marriage, shall have been continually absent from such person for the space of seven years, and shall not have been heard of by such person as being alive within that time provided the person contracting such subsequent marriage shall, before such marriage takes place, inform the person with whom such marriage is contracted of the real state of facts so far as the same are within his or her knowledge

(2) Whoever commits the offence under sub-section (1) having concealed from the person with whom the subsequent marriage is contracted, the fact of the former marriage, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine

learningObjectives: Understand bigamy and the voidness of subsequent marriage during the subsistence of a prior valid marriage under BNS s. 82(1).
Analyze the aggravated offence under s. 82(2) where the prior marriage is concealed from the subsequent spouse.
Examine statutory exceptions: judicial annulment and continuous seven-year absence with full disclosure.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 82 penalizes bigamy, providing that whoever, having a husband or wife living, marries in any case in which such marriage is void by reason of its taking place during the life of such spouse, faces imprisonment up to seven years and fine (sub-section 1); and if the fact of the former marriage is concealed from the subsequent spouse, imprisonment extends up to ten years and fine (sub-section 2).
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Monogamy is legally enforced by criminalizing bigamous unions where a spouse enters into a subsequent void marriage during the subsistence of an undissolved lawful marriage.
statutoryFramework: Chapter V — Of Offences against Women and Children, BNS s. 82 (corresponding to IPC ss. 494 and 495).
Sub-section (1): Basic bigamy — marrying during lifetime of living spouse where marriage is void by reason of prior marriage; punishable with imprisonment up to seven years and fine.

Sub-section (2): Aggravated bigamy — committing bigamy while concealing the fact of the former marriage from the person with whom subsequent marriage is contracted; imprisonment up to ten years and fine.

Exception: Does not extend to any person whose marriage has been declared void by a court of competent jurisdiction, nor to a person whose spouse has been continually absent for seven years and not heard of as alive, provided the real facts are disclosed to the prospective spouse.
essentialIngredients: The accused had a living husband or wife at the time of the subsequent marriage.
The first marriage was valid and legally subsisting.
The accused contracted a second marriage.
The second marriage is void by law by reason of taking place during the lifetime of the first spouse.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 82 consolidates the law on bigamy. Under sub-section (1), any person who contracts a second marriage while their first lawful spouse is alive commits bigamy if the personal law or general law applicable renders the second marriage void on that ground (such as the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 or Special Marriage Act, 1954). Strict proof of solemnization of both marriages according to customary rites or law is mandatory. Sub-section (2) incorporates the aggravated offence (formerly IPC 495) where the bigamist conceals the existing marriage from the new partner, carrying an enhanced penalty of up to ten years imprisonment. Two exceptions shield an accused: (i) where the prior marriage was dissolved or declared void by a competent court; and (ii) where the spouse has been absent for seven continuous years without being heard of, provided the facts are fully disclosed to the new partner.
examples: Teaching example (Basic bigamy): A man married under the Special Marriage Act marries another woman in a temple during the subsistence of his first marriage without divorcing his wife. The second marriage is void and he is guilty under s. 82(1).

Teaching example (Concealment of former marriage): A woman marries a man, falsely claiming she is a spinster, intentionally concealing her subsisting legal marriage. She is liable under s. 82(2) for aggravated bigamy with concealment.
distinctions: Section 82(1) vs Section 82(2): Sub-section (1) punishes bigamy as a status offence (up to 7 years); sub-section (2) punishes bigamy accompanied by fraudulent concealment from the innocent new partner (up to 10 years).

Bigamy (s. 82) vs Sham marriage (s. 83): In bigamy, a valid ceremony is gone through that would be lawful but for the existing spouse; in s. 83, the ceremony itself is known to be completely ineffective to create a lawful marriage.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused can escape bigamy charges by converting to another religion solely to contract a second marriage without dissolving the first.
Rule: A person married under a monogamous legal system cannot circumvent bigamy provisions by religious conversion; the prior marriage subsists until dissolved according to law.
Application: The first marriage was solemnized under personal laws mandating monogamy. No decree of divorce was granted.
Conclusion: The second marriage is void and the accused is liable under BNS s. 82(1).
